the measurement before any scene: the path from definition to reopen on the real library and route, the commit's latency, the restart maximum, the route's bytes and its server render rate (R11, D8).
S3 encrypting each object on the server with a key held in the key management service; here one key per organization (SSE-KMS) (10.6)

the bracketed mark saying how real a part is: [built] exists at a named pin, [proposed] is this design, still to be written, and [reduced: the platform's X] marks where the demo has something smaller than the platform's X, with a seam for X to return through; a tag may name the part it covers, as in [built: the rendering]; the platform's fourth, [deferred], designed for later, marks nothing in this record (reading note, 5; platform 5)
the six threat categories the table classifies by: spoofing, tampering, repudiation, information disclosure, denial of service, elevation of privilege (Microsoft) (10.4)
the process inside the container that restarts the binary in place, so a restart is a process restart, not a task replacement (5.2, 11.2).
made-up data that describes no real person or company; every number in the demo is computed from it (A10, 4.2)
the organization row's synthetic flag the provisioning script sets and no member can, required on every organization before a reset (section 9).
the operating-system functions, files, sockets and clocks, that a host may give a WebAssembly module, standardised as WASI (WASI); the parser gets none, only an input and an output (5.2, 6.4)

one recording of an act or of the whole run; the recording keeps one take of each act, each starting from the state the last ended in, and the per-take counts of 4.2, 11.2 and 11.3, N2's restarts among them, are of whole-run takes, up to twenty over ten rehearsals (appendix A, 4.2, 8)
the description ECS starts a task from, with its image, CPU, memory and environment; the rehearsal flag is one environment variable in the demo's (task definitions) (11.1, TH1)
ECS stopping a task and starting a new one from the image: pull, start, registration, health check; unmeasured against N2's 30 s, which is why a supervisor restarts in place (5.2, 11.2)
the cloud identity a task runs as; here one task role may connect as all five database roles, which is why the walls stop mistakes and not code inside the process (task IAM roles) (5.2, 10.5, AR2)
in fAuth, a separate group of users with its own sign-in settings; the demo has one per organization, northstar and the canary's (6.7)

the versions of this record the factory derives for particular readers, such as a reader's edition with presenter notes and this annotated edition; A1's "If wrong: the editions" means a different audience changes those, not the design (A1; Start here)
the person who commissions this record, approves it and owns every residual risk (cover, 10.4, 10.7)
who attacks, with their capability and motive, lettered TA; an operator script bug is one here (10.3)
a small marker left where data was deleted, so readers know it is gone; S06's deletion takes the platform's tombstone path, not the reset (8)
a line on a data-flow diagram where trust changes, lettered B; each crossing gets a threat row (7, 10.2)
a class of caller with a given power, lettered TL; the demo adds the canary's member, the operator's shell, the recording browser and role reset (10.2)

the components that must work for the invariants to hold; here the whole binary, the reset's guard and grants and the recorder's filter (Building Secure and Reliable Systems, chapter 6) (6.3, 6.7, 10.2)
a rule that a dangerous action needs a second person's approval; impossible with one founder, so accepted away (AR1)
the plain values, flags, lists and numbers, that the server computes for a renderer to draw (5.2)
an index that refuses a second row with the same key; on (organization, work, record, version) it turns two racing creates into one commit and one conflict (unique indexes) (7.2, 8)
a unit of compute, and two sizes of gigabyte: a GiB is 1,024 cubed bytes and a GB 1,000 cubed; the cost table uses both (11.2)
checking a token's signature against the cached key set without calling fAuth, so fAuth being down stops new sign-ins only (5.1, 6.9)
a web application firewall that filters requests by rules before they reach the application (AWS WAF); reduced away here, an address allowlist standing in during rehearsals (5.2, 10.4)
the W3C's accessibility guidelines; N12 checks every state of the demo's components at level AA (WCAG 2.2) (N12)
a portable binary that runs inside a host program which decides exactly which functions it may call, so it reaches nothing the host does not hand it (WebAssembly security) (5.2, 6.4)

dividing the window's bytes by the whole ten minutes, 1,140,000 ÷ 10 = 114,000 bytes a minute, rather than by the five minutes the included events span, which gives 228,000; act 3's patch adds the transfer-rate measure with it, a change to a calculation rather than to a style (R3, 7.1; platform 2; S02)
two separate grants, one to open a given case and one to run the app; a bare link carries neither (R6, 7.1)
Y Combinator, the startup programme the recording is made for; a partner there is the viewer the demo is judged by (A1, 4)

column1: G1: When is this goal done?
column2: G1 Six acts, one build. Done when acts 1 to 6 (§16) run end to end on one build digest on which S01 to S07 pass and the seven completeness clauses (§18) are ticked.

column1: G2: When is this goal done?
column2: G2 Two apps, one authoring path. Done when act 6 creates Spend Review through act 3's interface with no commit or deploy between, and the runtime has no branch on Northstar, Security or Finance (platform G1, R14; S07).

column1: G3: When is this goal done?
column2: G3 Work continues and reuses. Done when Jordan reopens Maya's case by its work id at its pinned publication with its records, a concurrent edit conflicts visibly, and his work for ops-runner-04 totals 210,000 bytes under its own id while Maya's 1,140,000 stand (S04).

column1: G4: When is this goal done?
column2: G4 Records persist, retry safely, conflict visibly. Done when EXP-002's decision survives refresh and restart, an ik-1 retry yields one revision and one audit event, a stale version conflicts, and ik-2 makes version 2 (S05; platform G4, D5).

column1: G5: When is this goal done?
column2: G5 Isolation shown with the canary. Done when the canary organization replays every call and link with Northstar's identifiers and gets nothing, not even metadata; a Security-only principal cannot read Finance; revocation stops derived and queued results (S01, S06; platform G5).

column1: G6: When is this goal done?
column2: G6 Nothing simulated passes as working. Done when every scene names its mechanism, every seeded, simulated or manual step is labeled and excluded from S07's acceptance measures, and the packet holds pins, digests, receipts, record outcomes and the rehearsal log (S07).

column1: G7: When is this goal done?
column2: G7 The demo grows into the platform. Done when each reduction names its seam (section 12) and every container maps onto a platform container under D1 to D14 (platform C16).

column1: A1: What is assumed, and what changes if it is wrong?
column2: A1 Audience. A YC partner watching, an engineer reading. If wrong: the editions.

column1: A2: What is assumed, and what changes if it is wrong?
column2: A2 Roles. Maya builds, Sarah reviews, Jordan reuses, under explicit grants. If wrong: grants move, authority holds.

column1: A3: What is assumed, and what changes if it is wrong?
column2: A3 One operator provisions, resets and restores. If wrong: section 11 names more.

column1: A4: What is assumed, and what changes if it is wrong?
column2: A4 Scale and rate. Two organizations, five accounts, four sessions, 0.8 actions/s sustained, four-action bursts. If wrong: remeasure.

column1: A5: What is assumed, and what changes if it is wrong?
column2: A5 Read-heavy, writes measured in rehearsal. If wrong: load-test commits.

column1: A6: What is assumed, and what changes if it is wrong?
column2: A6 Input caps. CSV 10 MiB, 100,000 rows; XLSX 5 MiB compressed, 50 MiB expanded, 10,000 rows × 32 columns per sheet: a tenth of the platform's A4 for CSV and half for XLSX, a reduction (6.4) still far above the fixtures, so the oversize refusal is real. If wrong: raise when measured.

column1: A7: What is assumed, and what changes if it is wrong?
column2: A7 Fan-out. Six linked views per filter. If wrong: bound query concurrency.

column1: A8: What is assumed, and what changes if it is wrong?
column2: A8 No SLA for a synthetic demo. If wrong: a pilot sets one.

column1: A9: What is assumed, and what changes if it is wrong?
column2: A9 One process, one host. If wrong: G7's seams are exercised.

column1: A10: What is assumed, and what changes if it is wrong?
column2: A10 Synthetic data only. If wrong: redo data classes and threats.

column1: A11: What is assumed, and what changes if it is wrong?
column2: A11 Platform D1 to D14 hold at the lock. If one moves: this record follows.

column1: A12: What is assumed, and what changes if it is wrong?
column2: A12 Sign-in. fAuth opens act 1 (K4); the platform's minimal login behind the same adapter is the fallback. If wrong: only act 1 changes.

column1: A13: What is assumed, and what changes if it is wrong?
column2: A13 Recording. Chrome, one profile an actor; sign-in is the platform's PKCE authorization-code flow as a registered fAuth client (platform SR2), one hand-added oauth_clients row. If wrong: the same-site refresh-cookie bridge, same adapter.

column1: A14: What is assumed, and what changes if it is wrong?
column2: A14 Spike first. The spike (section 5) passes before any rehearsal. If wrong: the recording waits.
N1 Scalability. Not required beyond the envelope; scale is the platform's N1 through R10's seams; A6's caps enforced (S06).

N2 Availability. No SLA (A8), no lost scene: after a process restart saved work reopens within 30 s (one restart a whole-run take, the maximum over twenty), so one step is redone, not an act; platform-caused retakes in the last three rehearsals: zero.

N3 Latency at the client, the platform's targets measured, not promised: navigation p50 250 ms, p99 1 s; six-view refresh p50 500 ms, p99 2 s; commit p50 300 ms, p99 1 s; revocation within 5 s; sample sizes in 11.3; jobs show state within 1 s.

N4 Fault tolerance. Safety: no fault serves Northstar's data to the canary, widens authority, duplicates a record or shows an unreceipted number. Liveness: a committed record survives a restart; a provider outage leaves navigation, queries and forms working, generation failing visibly within 1 s; a restore is timed and reported (S06).
N5 Consistency. The platform's N5 holds: linearizable record commands, compare-and-set publication and adoption, read-your-write, revocation within 5 s (C07, C09, C10).

N6 Accuracy. The fixtures recompute server-side in integers, 1,140,000 bytes, 900,000 unmatched, 114,000 a minute, 210,000 and 21,000 for Jordan, 64,000 cents and the 45,000-cent queue; every shown number equals its receipt (S02, S04, S05; platform N6).
N7 Security. R8's replay and every S06 row run as tests, denial and absence of effect captured.
N8 Privacy. Synthetic data only (A10); the composer's real-data disclosure stays off; every provider request is inspected (C12).

N9 Maintainability. Zero commits and deploys between acts 3 and 6: one build digest, both definition digests under it, no organization, space or app name in the runtime's control flow (S07; platform N9; C13).
N10 Cost. Unknown yet; the requirement is the meter, tokens a call and hosting a rehearsal, reported with the recording.
N11 Sustainability. Not required separately; N10's meter bounds it.
N12 Accessibility. S01's keyboard path and an automated WCAG 2.2 AA check on every state of the demo's components (platform N12).

column1: SR1: What must hold, and how is it tested?
column2: SR1 The reset MUST exist only under flag and role, restore digest-matched states, keep audit (M1 to M4, M15, M16). Tests: 404 per build; a tampered state 412.

column1: SR2: What must hold, and how is it tested?
column2: SR2 The canary suite MUST run per build and at both ends of every take, every replay 404 against an identifier its owner resolved with 200 in that take, behind M29's allowlist (M7, M8, M25, M26, M29). Test: no non-404, none without its 200.

column1: SR3: What must hold, and how is it tested?
column2: SR3 Sign-in MUST use the registered client, one redirect URI, dry-run per take (M5, M6). Test: a wrong URI.

column1: SR4: What must hold, and how is it tested?
column2: SR4 Packet and recording MUST hold no header, cookie, token or key; the packet's manifest digest anchored before delivery (M11, M12, M30, M31). Check: pattern scan; the anchor.

column1: SR5: What must hold, and how is it tested?
column2: SR5 Operator keys MUST stay in the keychain, then die; operator actions and build digest audited (M9, M10, M13, M14, M27, M28). Check: the packet.

column1: SR6: What must hold, and how is it tested?
column2: SR6 Revocation and reset MUST reach every tab within 5 s; the sandbox dies first; injection and unknown operations fail whole (M17 to M24). Test: S06's rows.

column1: SI7: What must always hold, and which component enforces it?
column2: SI7 (safety) Rehearsal: the reset exists only under the flag with role reset, restores only a digest-matched state, never deletes audit or sessions; enforced by reset's grants (none on audit or sessions), tested per build, and P11's guard.

column1: SI8: What must always hold, and which component enforces it?
column2: SI8 (safety) Evidence: the packet holds only what the browser received and the operator views returned, every number matched to its receipt, no credential; enforced by P10's filter.

column1: D1: What was decided, which door is it, and what does it serve?
column2: Decision: One process runs the four roles, each its own database role; the parser a WebAssembly module in the worker · Door: two-way · Serves: N9, N2, G7 · Cost: one failure domain · Alternative: four deployments · Section: 6, 11 · The platform's: D11 · D1, one process. Drivers: A3, N9, G7, N7. Options: (A) the platform's roles as separate deployments, which optimises for the production shape but gives one founder eight things to restart during a take, losing against A3 and N2; (B) one process, one database credential, the shared-database antipattern, which optimises for simplicity but lets the role handling model output write a publication, losing against N7; (chosen) one process, each role its own database role, the parser a WebAssembly module in the worker (platform D11). Chosen because D11 allows it and the write grants survive the collapse (AR2). Good: one binary, one digest (N9). Bad: one fault stops all. Confirmed by the per-build test that workspace and worker cannot write a publication through their pools, which code holding the task role escapes (AR2).

column1: D2: What was decided, which door is it, and what does it serve?
column2: Decision: One PostgreSQL instance, one S3 bucket in the platform's region; the organization id in every key from row one · Door: one-way for the keys · Serves: N7, G5, G7 · Cost: no standby · Alternative: SQLite and files · Section: 8, 11 · The platform's: D3, D4; its 11.1 steps 1 to 3 true at birth · D2, the organization id in every key. Drivers: N7, G5, G7. Options: one organization per rehearsal (nothing for the canary to replay, losing against G5); a demo schema with the id added later (the seam becomes a migration, losing against G7); (chosen) the platform's keys from row one. Chosen because isolation is the recording's claim and keys cannot be retrofitted on camera. Good: the canary suite runs unchanged. Bad: one instance, no standby. Confirmed by the suite each take (R8).

column1: D3: What was decided, which door is it, and what does it serve?
column2: Decision: The platform's AppDefinition, admission, publication and record command code, no fork · Door: one-way: what both apps are made of · Serves: G2, N9, G7 · Cost: full admission at demo scale · Alternative: a demo-only format · Section: 6, 9 · The platform's: D1, D2, D5, D9, D14 · D3, the platform's code, no fork. Drivers: G2, N9, G7. Options: a demo-only definition format (act 6 becomes a second implementation, losing against G2); a demo-scale fork of admission (every contract reopens, losing against N9); (chosen) the platform's AppDefinition, admission, publication and command code. Chosen because two apps through one path (§18) proves nothing unless the path is the product's. Good: N9's zero deploys is structural. Bad: full admission at demo scale. Confirmed by S07's packet and the silent deploy log.

column1: D4: What was decided, which door is it, and what does it serve?
column2: Decision: fAuth's hosted sign-in (A12; K4), the platform's minimal login behind the same adapter as fallback · Door: two-way at the protocol · Serves: R1, N7 · Cost: a second deployment, its cookies · Alternative: an organization dropdown, refused · Section: 6, 10 · The platform's: D6 · D4, the identity adapter. Drivers: A12, R1, N7, G7. Options: (C) an organization dropdown, which optimises for a short act 1 and is not a reduction, losing against G6; (D) fAuth's hosted sign-in, a real tenant boundary on camera for a second visual language and a client row; (E) the platform's minimal login, one fewer dependency; (chosen) the adapter with D behind it and E as the fallback (K4). Chosen because the token contract binds the demo and the provider does not (platform D6), and because the canary's denial (G5) and revocation then rest on a tenant boundary the demo did not build. Good: only act 1 changes; no password reaches the platform. Bad: a second deployment for one act, a client row by hand. Confirmed by the canary's token replay and the dry sign-in against both adapters on every build (M6; 11.1).

column1: D7: What was decided, which door is it, and what does it serve?
column2: Decision: The integrity rule: every scene names its mechanism and captures evidence; nothing simulated passes (G6) · Door: one-way once submitted · Serves: G6, G1, N9 · Cost: retakes · Alternative: a staged recording · Section: 7, 13 · The platform's: C16, R14 · D7, the integrity rule. Drivers: G6, S07. Options: (F) a staged demo, fixtures wherever the path is slow, which optimises for a smooth take but makes the video the evidence, losing against G6 and R9; (chosen) every scene's mechanism named, its evidence captured, nothing simulated passes. Chosen because the partner's question is whether the second app is real. Good: a packet that outlives the video. Bad: retakes; one-way once submitted, a packet cannot be relabeled after YC has it. Confirmed by S07's packet checked against the build digest (M28).

column1: D5: What was decided, which door is it, and what does it serve?
column2: Decision: The platform's nine kinds as defined (platform 6.5) plus the CIDR lookup and the integer currency operators (C13); no kind added for the demo · Door: two-way: a kind is a release · Serves: N3, N6, G2 · Cost: 426 B of route headroom · Alternative: a kind added for the demo · Section: 6 · The platform's: D10, D1

column1: D6: What was decided, which door is it, and what does it serve?
column2: Decision: Organizations, members, policies and fixtures provisioned by script (fAuth's tenant steps) · Door: two-way · Serves: G5, G6, R4 · Cost: kept true by hand · Alternative: administration pages · Section: 11 · The platform's: D6; D2's policy

column1: D8: What was decided, which door is it, and what does it serve?
column2: Decision: The spike before any scene (R11) · Door: two-way · Serves: G1, N3, A14 · Cost: the first rehearsal waits · Alternative: scenes first · Section: 5, 11 · The platform's: its spike (A14)

column1: D9: What was decided, which door is it, and what does it serve?
column2: Decision: The platform's code flow with PKCE as a registered fAuth client, one oauth_clients row added by hand (A13) · Door: two-way · Serves: R1, N7 · Cost: a row fAuth has no API for · Alternative: the same-site refresh-cookie bridge · Section: 10, 11 · The platform's: D6's handoff

column1: D10: What was decided, which door is it, and what does it serve?
column2: Decision: One ECS task in one region by default, so the platform's deployment carries over; else one virtual machine · Door: two-way · Serves: G7, N10 · Cost: money, metered (N10) · Alternative: a virtual machine; the founder's machine · Section: 11 · The platform's: D15 (one region), reduced to one task

column1: TH1: What is the threat, and the response?
column2: DFD element or boundary crossed: B2, P11, P2, DS1, F17, F18 · STRIDE: Elevation of privilege · Threat statement: A deploy mistake (TA9, TA11) setting the rehearsal flag in the platform's task definition can expose the reset to real organizations, which leads to their rows replaced by a fixture state, negatively impacting AS2, AS3, AS12 · Invariant at stake: SI7 · Existing control: none · Response: mitigate · Mitigation: M1 prevent: P9 creates role reset, never a migration; the route registers only when flag and role both exist. M2 detect: every build starts the image under the platform's task definition and asserts 404 and no reset role · Likelihood: Low · Impact: High · Status: proposed · Residual risk: Low

column1: TH2: What is the threat, and the response?
column2: DFD element or boundary crossed: B2 at the operator prefix, DS2, P9, P11, F16, F19 · STRIDE: Tampering · Threat statement: A fixture-state writer (TA12) with the operator prefix can alter a state, which leads to a take starting from state no clean take produced, negatively impacting AS9, AS10 · Invariant at stake: SI7, SI8 · Existing control: S3 object versions [built] · Response: mitigate · Mitigation: M3 prevent: the state's digest, SHA-256 over manifest and build digest, lives in the pin file in the repository at the build's tag, apart from DS2; the reset recomputes it, 412 on a mismatch. M4 detect: P10 diffs each restored manifest, publication and approval digests included, against its capture (s3 no publication, s4 publication 1 only) · Likelihood: Low · Impact: High · Status: proposed · Residual risk: Low

column1: TH3: What is the threat, and the response?
column2: DFD element or boundary crossed: B1, EE1, P1, P2, F2 · STRIDE: Spoofing; Tampering · Threat statement: An outsider (TA1) with a lure link, or P9 (TA11) with a wrong or second redirect URI, can land the code elsewhere or sign the recording browser in as another principal, which leads to a session not Maya's on camera, negatively impacting AS1, AS11 · Invariant at stake: SI1 · Existing control: fAuth's PKCE S256 page [built]; platform M6, M7 [proposed] · Response: mitigate · Mitigation: M5 prevent: P9 inserts the client row from its manifest with one same-site redirect URI (A13); a public PKCE client, the code verifier its proof, no secret to keep. M6 detect: the pre-take dry sign-in asserts the URI and state; failure stops the take · Likelihood: Low · Impact: High · Status: proposed · Residual risk: Low: AR4

column1: TH4: What is the threat, and the response?
column2: DFD element or boundary crossed: B7, EE1, P2, P4, DS1, F1 to F3, F10 · STRIDE: Information disclosure; Elevation of privilege · Threat statement: The canary's member (TA2), replaying every call with Northstar's identifiers on the instance holding both organizations, can reach a Northstar row through a handler missing its scope, which leads to one organization's data served to another, negatively impacting AS3, AS4 · Invariant at stake: SI1 · Existing control: tenant_id from fAuth's token [built]; platform M1 [proposed] · Response: mitigate · Mitigation: M7 prevent: platform M1 on one instance: the organization only from the session, row-level security everywhere, two data keys. M8 detect: the canary suite per build and at both ends of every take on that take's identifiers, each replay paired with the owner's 200 and answered 404 before data (F10), both filed; a non-404 or a replay without its 200 fails the take · Likelihood: High · Impact: High · Status: proposed · Residual risk: Low

column1: TH5: What is the threat, and the response?
column2: DFD element or boundary crossed: B2 at EE2, P9, P11, DS1, F14 to F16 · STRIDE: Elevation of privilege; Repudiation · Threat statement: The operator (TA9), or whoever holds the shell's keys (AS12; TA1 with the laptop), can invite a principal into any tenant, change the client row, reset, revoke or set policy alone and deny it, which leads to a member nobody invited and state changed by one person, negatively impacting AS12, AS1, AS7 · Invariant at stake: SI1, SI2, SI5 · Existing control: fAuth's invite-only tenants [built]; platform M3, M14 [proposed] · Response: mitigate; accept the one-person case (AR1, AR3) · Mitigation: M9 prevent: AS12's keys live in the keychain, the AWS role assumed per session, read by P9 at run time, never in repository, history or log; the owner credential creates the roles once, then rotates into Secrets Manager with no standing reader; fAuth's database credential rotates after the one insert; the operator role lasts one take, granted with the take's id as reason, every call carrying the operator's principal. M10 detect: the pre-take assertion compares fAuth's users and the membership rows with P9's manifest; P10 lists every operator action against the script; an extra one fails the take · Likelihood: Medium · Impact: High · Status: proposed · Residual risk: Medium: AR1, AR3

column1: TH6: What is the threat, and the response?
column2: DFD element or boundary crossed: EE1, P8, P10, B1, F12 · STRIDE: Information disclosure · Threat statement: The operator (TA9) exporting an unsanitised log, or the audience (TA13) seeing a callback URL, a terminal or developer tools on camera, can obtain a cookie, state, a code or a key, which leads to a credential handed to every recipient, negatively impacting AS10, AS11, AS12 · Invariant at stake: SI8 · Existing control: none · Response: mitigate · Mitigation: M11 prevent: P10 reads only Chrome's sanitised export, keeps status, request id and named /v1/ bodies, drops every remaining header, refuses a capture still carrying Cookie, Set-Cookie or Authorization; no developer tools or terminals on camera, the address bar cut at the callback; every secret dies after the last take (10.6). M12 detect: the platform's M42 scan over the packet; a second viewer of the cut · Likelihood: Medium · Impact: High · Status: proposed · Residual risk: Low

column1: TH7: What is the threat, and the response?
column2: DFD element or boundary crossed: B2, DS1, DS2, P2 · STRIDE: Denial of service · Threat statement: A hardware fault or a wrong destroy (TA9) on one instance without standby can lose everything since the pre-rehearsal snapshot, audit included, which leads to a lost rehearsal and a hole in the audit trail, negatively impacting AS3, AS7, AS10 · Invariant at stake: SI5 · Existing control: RDS snapshots, S3 versions [built]; platform M22 [proposed] · Response: mitigate; accept one host (AR2) · Mitigation: M13 prevent: a snapshot before each rehearsal, the bucket's versions, the chain head anchored to Object Lock every 15 minutes (platform AR9), P10's copy of the take's audit. M14 detect: S06's timed restore into an isolated environment, destroyed within the hour, then chain verification against the anchors · Likelihood: Low · Impact: High · Status: proposed · Residual risk: Medium: AR2, RPO one rehearsal

column1: AR1: What risk was accepted, and why?
column2: Accepted risk: No two-person rule and no breakglass: the operator self-grants the role and resets, revokes and sets policy alone · Reason: one founder (A3); every action listed against the script (M10); synthetic data

column1: AR2: What risk was accepted, and why?
column2: Accepted risk: One host and one process: a compromise of the process is every role and both organizations; RPO one rehearsal · Reason: D1, D10; the grants bound bugs; the canary suite only detects the rest

column1: AR3: What risk was accepted, and why?
column2: Accepted risk: The operator's shell holds AS12's keys · Reason: fAuth has no federation for a script and no client API at b750ca53 (platform AR4); the keychain, single use where possible and destruction after delivery bound it

column1: AR4: What risk was accepted, and why?
column2: Accepted risk: The client row and its redirect URI are added by hand · Reason: fAuth has no API for it (A13); the dry sign-in catches a wrong row

column1: AR5: What risk was accepted, and why?
column2: Accepted risk: A demo-only route ships in the platform's binary · Reason: dead without flag and role, proven every build (M2); a second binary breaks N9's one digest

column1: TH8: What is the threat, and the response?
column2: DFD element or boundary crossed: B4, P11, P4, DS1, F7, F18 · STRIDE: Tampering; Denial of service · Threat statement: The operator (TA9) resetting while a command is in flight, or double-clicking, can delete a record between a command's outcome lookup and its insert, which leads to an outcome without its record or a dead take's row surviving into the next, negatively impacting AS3 · Invariant at stake: SI3, SI7 · Existing control: platform M40's locks [proposed] · Response: mitigate · Mitigation: M15 prevent: the reset takes each organization's membership row FOR UPDATE in the transaction that deletes, serialising with every command's FOR SHARE (6.7); it is 409 while any job is claimed; it carries an Idempotency-Key; it bumps the epoch, so a command queued before it is denied at execution. M16 detect: the pre-take assertion counts rows against the state's manifest; a mismatch is a retake · Likelihood: Medium · Impact: Medium · Status: proposed · Residual risk: Low

column1: TH9: What is the threat, and the response?
column2: DFD element or boundary crossed: B1, DS4, P2, F4 · STRIDE: Elevation of privilege · Threat statement: Jordan after Maya revokes his grant (TA3), or a cookie from a prior take, can keep calling for the session's remaining life, sessions surviving the reset, which leads to a read after revocation on camera or a prior take's principal acting in the next, negatively impacting AS1, AS3 · Invariant at stake: SI4 · Existing control: platform M24 [proposed] · Response: mitigate · Mitigation: M17 prevent: the epoch on every request (F4) with no cache before it, the canvas refresh at 5 s, and the reset's epoch bump, so every open tab re-authorizes within 5 s of a reset; a take of act 1 starts from a signed-out profile. M18 detect: the denial's time against the revocation's in the rehearsal log (N3's 5 s), in the packet · Likelihood: Medium · Impact: Medium · Status: proposed · Residual risk: Low: a cookie of an unrevoked actor acts until sign-out

column1: TH10: What is the threat, and the response?
column2: DFD element or boundary crossed: B6, P5, P6, P2 · STRIDE: Denial of service; Elevation of privilege · Threat statement: A 4 MiB XLSX under A6's compressed cap, or any file a builder drops (TA3), inflating past 50 MiB in a WebAssembly module inside the one process can exhaust the host's memory, and a parser exploit escaping the module can run with every role's pool, both data keys and the provider key through the one task role, which leads to every role stopping, not one worker (D1), or to both organizations read and the operator's secrets taken, negatively impacting AS3, AS4, AS5, AS12 · Invariant at stake: SI2, SI6 · Existing control: platform M8, M9 [proposed] · Response: mitigate; accept the one process (AR2) · Mitigation: M19 prevent: the module's memory cap and fuel (A6) are enforced by the runtime below the task's 8 GiB (11.2), so the process survives the module; the byte caps refuse before parsing; the module has no system interface and no path to the task's credentials endpoint. M20 detect: the refusal and its reason captured (S06); a killed or crashed module audited; both parsers fuzzed in CI; a restart in a take is logged with the step redone (N2) · Likelihood: High (exhaustion); Low (escape) · Impact: Medium; High · Status: proposed · Residual risk: Low; Medium: AR2

column1: TH11: What is the threat, and the response?
column2: DFD element or boundary crossed: B5, P5, EE4 · STRIDE: Tampering · Threat statement: S06's "export every secret" field (TA5), sent to the provider among the synthetic rows on camera, can steer the proposal, which leads to a misleading definition or an attempted operation outside D5's set, negatively impacting AS3 · Invariant at stake: SI2 · Existing control: platform M26 [proposed]; the renderer admits no markup [built: review 4.3] · Response: mitigate · Mitigation: M21 prevent: platform M26 unchanged, the field a delimited data value. M22 detect: the field runs as a test on every build, and the take's admission report, captured, shows the proposal validated whole with the field as data · Likelihood: High · Impact: Medium · Status: proposed · Residual risk: Low: platform AR11

column1: TH12: What is the threat, and the response?
column2: DFD element or boundary crossed: B3, P3, P5; platform F15 · STRIDE: Tampering · Threat statement: The model (TA6), or the labeled fixture in the spike (TA11, a script bug), can propose an operation or kind outside D5's eleven, or the fixture can pass as generated, which leads to a draft rendering an unknown kind or a seeded proposal counted as working, negatively impacting AS2, AS10 · Invariant at stake: SI2, SI8 · Existing control: the renderer refuses a computed kind [built: BUILD-610, review 4.3]; platform M30 [proposed] · Response: mitigate · Mitigation: M23 prevent: platform M30 unchanged, admission failing whole, nothing partial stored; the fixture proposal carries a fixture label admission writes into its report, so P10 marks the scene seeded (G6). M24 detect: the admission report in the packet names the registry version and every refused kind · Likelihood: High · Impact: Medium · Status: proposed · Residual risk: Low

column1: TH13: What is the threat, and the response?
column2: DFD element or boundary crossed: B4, P4, DS1, F7, F8 · STRIDE: Spoofing; Tampering · Threat statement: The canary's member (TA2) or Jordan (TA3) posting ik-1 with Northstar's work id, or the next take reusing ik-1, can read another principal's outcome or receive a dead take's, which leads to a decision read across principals or a stale outcome answering a new take, negatively impacting AS3 · Invariant at stake: SI3 · Existing control: none · Response: mitigate · Mitigation: M25 prevent: platform M32's key (organization, principal, work, command, key), so the canary's post is 404 at P2 and Jordan's finds nothing; the reset deletes outcomes and flushes the cache, so a key crosses no take (section 9). M26 detect: key conflicts audited; the canary's and Jordan's ik-1 in the packet · Likelihood: Medium · Impact: Medium · Status: proposed · Residual risk: Low

column1: TH14: What is the threat, and the response?
column2: DFD element or boundary crossed: B2 at the task definition, P2, P10, F13 · STRIDE: Tampering; Repudiation · Threat statement: The operator (TA9) deploying a fix between acts 3 and 6 can change the build under the recording, which leads to N9's claim, one digest for both apps, failing unseen, negatively impacting AS10 · Invariant at stake: SI8 · Existing control: none · Response: mitigate · Mitigation: M27 prevent: one image digest for the whole recording; a new build is a new rehearsal (11.1). M28 detect: P10 reads the task's image digest at the take's start and end and the deploy log between them; a difference fails acceptance · Likelihood: Low · Impact: High · Status: proposed · Residual risk: Low

column1: TH15: What is the threat, and the response?
column2: DFD element or boundary crossed: B9, EE2, P9, P10, F12, F14 to F16 · STRIDE: Information disclosure; Elevation of privilege · Threat statement: Whoever controls the operator's machine (TA1 by malware, a browser extension or theft; TA9) can take every key, every actor's session, the unfiltered export and the pin file at once, which leads to any principal in either organization and every operator power, negatively impacting AS1, AS11, AS12, AS13 · Invariant at stake: SI1, SI8 · Existing control: the OS keychain prompt; full-disk encryption [built] · Response: mitigate; accept the one machine (AR3) · Mitigation: M30 prevent: a fresh Chrome profile per actor with sync and extensions off, destroyed after the last take; the sanitised export plus P10's filter, the raw file hashed, filtered and deleted in one step; the platform key deleted from the keychain once the tenants exist; full-disk encryption; the machine off the network except while a rehearsal runs. M31 detect: the packet's manifest digest written as an audit event under the Object Lock anchor after each take, so an edited packet no longer matches; fAuth's user list and the session rows against the manifest before each take (M10); sign-out everywhere after each take · Likelihood: Medium · Impact: High · Status: proposed · Residual risk: Low

column1: The summary names three one-way doors: the organization id in every key (D2), the platform's definition and command code (D3), and the integrity rule once the packet is submitted (D7). Before reading 5.3, write for each what reversing it a month after the recording would require, and whose action it would need. Then say why the hand-added client row (D9), awkward as it is, is not on the list.
column2: D2 needs our own action, but on everything stored: the organization id is in every key in every store from the first row, so reversing it means a migration of all stored data and every reference to it, and the isolation the recording showed would then describe keys the system no longer has ("keys cannot be retrofitted on camera", 12.2). D3 needs our own action too: a second implementation of the definition, admission and command code, after which every contract reopens and act 6 would have proved an implementation that no longer runs (12.2). D7 needs someone else's: the packet is with YC, so relabeling a step would take the recipient's action, not ours ("a packet cannot be relabeled after YC has it", 12.2). Two doors are one-way because of what a reversal would touch, the third because the reversal is out of our hands. D9 is one row and one redirect URI in fAuth's database: replacing it, with the refresh-cookie bridge or a future client API (13.2's POST /manage/oauth-clients), is our action on one adapter's input and touches nothing the platform stores, which is why 5.3 marks it two-way (1, 5.3, 12.2).

column1: Write a fourth shortcut in section 2's form, for act 5, share and reuse: the fastest way to make Jordan's reopening of Maya's case look right on screen, other than section 2's third, which already has one session play everyone. Then name what it leaves untested, by the goal or requirement it fails, and the observation in the packet that would expose it.
column2: One version: give Jordan a copy of Maya's case under a new id; the screen shows the same findings. A copy is a different work id, so G3's "reopens Maya's case by its work id at its pinned publication with its records" fails, and so does R6's same id, records and pin. It also outlives revocation, because revoking Jordan's grant on Maya's case does not touch his copy, so R6's "revocation denies later results" cannot be shown, and a concurrent edit cannot conflict because the two cases share no record (G3's visible conflict). The packet would expose it twice. Act 5's "both work ids" must be Maya's own id, reopened under Jordan's session, and his new one for ops-runner-04; with the copy, the case Jordan opens carries an id Maya never had. And no denial follows the revocation (5 act 5's "Captured"; 7.1 act 5; S04). Any answer is right that names a mechanism replaced by its appearance and the identity or denial that the evidence would then lack (2).

column1: It is the morning of a rehearsal and sign-in is broken, in one of three ways: (a) fAuth's service is down; (b) the provisioning script inserted the client row with a typo in its redirect URI; (c) the head learns that fAuth at the pin cannot hold a registered client at all. From section 3 alone, name the assumption each case breaks, if any, and what you would do. Then derive what the assumptions only imply: for (a), what must already be true of the design for A12's "only act 1 changes" to hold; for (c), which goal A13's fallback strains, and why. Check (a) against 6.9 and 11.1, and (b) against SR3 and 11.4, when you reach them.
column2: (a) breaks the first half of A12, fAuth opening act 1: wait for fAuth, or switch before the take to A12's fallback, the platform's minimal login behind the same adapter; either way only act 1's scene changes. For "only act 1 changes" to hold, a session must not need fAuth once it exists: the platform keeps its own sessions and checks fAuth's tokens without calling fAuth. It does: sessions are PostgreSQL rows that live 12 h, tokens are verified offline against the cached key set, and the fallback is switched before a take, never during it (5.1, 6.1, 6.9, 11.1; 11.4's fAuth row: act 1 waits, later acts continue). (b) breaks no assumption: A13 holds, since fAuth can hold the row, and the row is simply wrong, so nothing in the design moves. Correct the row by hand and prove sign-in before the camera rolls; the record's check is the dry sign-in, which stops a take until it passes (SR3, 6.1; 11.4's row for the provisioning script's output), and D9 being a two-way door is why a hand fix is enough. (c) breaks A13: its fallback is the same-site refresh-cookie bridge behind the same adapter, so act 1's mechanism changes and D9 would be revisited. The goal it strains is G7: the bridge is a session contract the platform never ships, so either the demo signs in in a way the platform does not, or the platform carries it for one demo, and 12.2 rejects it for that reason (12.2's table, 12.3). The three mornings look alike, "sign-in is broken", and the assumptions separate them: one has a fallback, one is an error to correct, one moves a decision (3.3, 5.3, 12.2).

column1: 4.2's basis is ten rehearsals, each one whole-run take filmed at most twice, and a 30-minute rehearsal holds about 360 interactions: about 200 six-view refreshes (1,200 operations), 40 navigations, 20 commits, and edits and uploads for the rest. Rebuild the 360 and the 1,200, and work out how many edits and uploads remain. Then, before reading 11.3, decide over how many rehearsals you would pool navigations and commits to report a p99, and count the samples that would lie above the p99 in each case, compared with the 200 refreshes of one whole-run take.
column2: 30 minutes is 1,800 s; one action every 5 s is 360 interactions; 200 refreshes times six views is 1,200 query operations; 360 − 200 − 40 − 20 = 100 edits and uploads. A p99 leaves one sample in a hundred above it, so one whole-run take's 200 refreshes leave 2 above it, enough to say something, while its 40 navigations or 20 commits leave less than one, so their "p99" would just be the slowest sample. Pooling ten rehearsals, one whole run each, gives 400 navigations, 4 above the p99, and 200 commits, 2 above, which is what 11.3 does; the refresh needs no pooling because one take of the whole run already holds 200 (4.2, N3, 11.3). The counts are per whole run: a take of one act holds only that act's share of them.

column1: Rebuild a take's burst from 5.2's rules: how many query operations one filter change puts at the data service, how many run and how many wait, how many waves, and how long at 100 ms a warm operation. Then redo it for a version of Spend Review with eight linked views during a scene where two actors act at once: the operations, the waves, the time, any 429s, and the warm operation time at which N3's 2 s would stop holding.
column2: One actor, six linked views: six operations; the data service admits two of an organization's at once, so 2 run and 4 wait, three waves, 0.3 s at 100 ms, inside N3's 2 s (5.2); the waves are why 6.3 puts the ceiling at a warm operation of about 650 ms, three waves inside 2 s. Two actors, eight views: 16 operations in one organization, 2 running and 14 waiting; 429s begin only past 20 waiting (5.2; platform 6.3), so none is refused; eight waves of two, 0.8 s at 100 ms, still inside 2 s; and N3's 2 s stops holding at a warm operation of about 2 s ÷ 8 = 250 ms. The envelope's burst of 24 is different in kind: 22 waiting is two past the 20, those two are the 429s, and that is why four simultaneous actors are not a take (5.2, 6.3, 11.2).

column1: 5.2 has the supervisor restart the binary "inside the load balancer's grace of three failed checks 10 s apart". (a) From those two numbers, how soon after a crash can the third failed check come? (b) Predict what the take sees if the binary takes 40 s to come back. (c) Act 4's restart drill falls between acts 3 and 6, where N9 allows no deploy. From N9's own wording, decide what a change must alter to count as a deploy, and so whether the drill is one; then design the check that would tell a restart from a deploy in the evidence, and compare it with 6.7 and TH14 when you reach them.
column2: (a) Checks come every 10 s, so the first failure lands up to 10 s after the crash and the third 20 s after the first: between about 20 and 30 s after the crash the target is taken out of service (5.2; the load balancer's failure threshold). (b) At 40 s the target has been taken out of service, so the load balancer stops sending it requests and Maya's reload fails until the binary is back and the checks pass again (11.4's first row: the target re-registers on the next check); the case reopens later than N2's 30 s, and a miss of N2 ends the take (11.1, step 5), so act 4 is retaken from s3, and the acts after it with it (8). One more consequence is an inference the record implies without stating it: 5.2 puts the restart inside the grace so that it triggers "no task replacement", so a restart past the grace may bring the task replacement as well, the sequence nobody has timed against 30 s (RK8). (c) N9 asks for one build digest for both apps and no deploy between acts 3 and 6, so what it forbids is a change of the image that runs. A restart, in place or even as a new task, runs the same image digest, so it is not a deploy, as 6.7 says outright: "a task start on the same image digest, act 4's restart drill, is not a deploy". The check follows from that definition: read the task's image digest at the take's start and end, and the deploy log between them. A restart leaves both unchanged; a deploy changes the digest or writes to the log, and either fails acceptance. That is TH14's M28, run by the evidence recorder (6.7, N9, TH14).

column1: Act 2 must capture one oversize refusal (S06). The platform record's example of a bomb is a 9 MiB XLSX that inflates past 100 MiB (platform 7.1). Explain why a 9 MiB file could never test the demo's expansion cap. Then, before reading 7.1's act 2, predict what a 4 MiB file that inflates past 50 MiB tests instead: which of A6's limits fires, and where; what stops and what survives; what the job and the recording show. Finally say what the module's 2 GiB memory cap is for, if a limit fires long before it.
column2: A6 caps an XLSX at 5 MiB compressed and 50 MiB expanded, and a file's compressed size is known before anything opens it, so a 9 MiB file is turned away at the size check and never expands: it tests the byte cap, not the expansion cap (appendix C confirms it in TH10's M19: "the byte caps refuse before parsing"). In the platform, whose compressed cap is 10 MiB (platform A4), the same file does reach the parser, which is why it is the platform's example. The 4 MiB file passes the byte cap, so the parser starts inflating it inside its WebAssembly sandbox and meets the 50 MiB expanded cap: the parse stops there and the file is refused, the job carries the reason, the import fails visibly, the refusal is captured, and the process and the take carry on (7.1 act 2; 11.4's parser row). The 2 GiB memory cap never fires in this case: it is the backstop. If a parse ever got past the expanded cap, the runtime would still stop the module at 2 GiB, and the task's 8 GiB is sized so that 2 GiB fits beside everything else the process holds, so even then the module, not the process, would die (7.1, 11.2; TH10's M19). What the file tests is the bounded parser that is the reduction's seam (6.4) and the property one process makes critical: a bad file costs a refusal, never the process (TH10).

column1: The reset keeps sessions and bumps the membership epoch. Predict what would change if it deleted every session row instead and left the epoch alone: for the take procedure, for fAuth, for role reset's grants, and for a tab still open from the previous take.
column2: The procedure: every actor would have to sign in again through fAuth's page after every reset, instead of once within the idle hour (11.1, step 3, which relies on "the reset keeps sessions"). fAuth: more sign-ins per rehearsal push against its login limit, which the cold start already has to raise (11.1; 11.4's limiter row). The grants: role reset would need a grant on the session table, which SI7 forbids ("never deletes audit or sessions", enforced by reset's grants), so the most dangerous role in the demo would reach identity rows. The open tab: it would be denied at its next request because its session is gone, the same safety the epoch bump gives, bought with re-sign-ins. The epoch bump gets that safety without touching sessions: every open tab re-authorizes within 5 s against the restored membership rows and no session is lost (6.7, 8, TH9).

column1: In act 6's lost response, ik-1 is posted twice, both times with expected version 0, though after the first post the record is at version 1. Suppose P4 compared the expected version before looking for the stored outcome: predict what the second post would return and what Maya and the packet would then show, and say what finding the outcome first protects. Then compare the two ways a client can recover from a lost response, retrieving the outcome by key first (section 9's rule) or re-submitting under the same key (the path the script forces): what would each leave in the packet, and which part of act 6's claim does only the second exercise?
column2: Version first, the second post would fail: its expected version 0 no longer matches the record's version 1, so P4 would roll back and answer 409 with the recovery view, as it does for the stale edit under ik-3 (7.2, step 5). Maya would be told that her own decision conflicted with itself, and the packet would hold a 409 for a command that had in fact committed: the retry would look like a conflict, and G4's duplicate-safe retry could not be shown. Finding the stored outcome first is what makes a retry safe whatever the client believes: the first post stored its outcome under ik-1 in the same transaction as version 1 (F7), so the second finds it before any version check and returns version 1 (F7, F8; step 4), while authorization still runs again (F4), because a key names a command, not a permission. Retrieving first would leave one POST and one GET by key: it shows that an outcome is stored, but the server never sees the command twice. The forced re-submission leaves two POSTs under one key against one record revision, one audit event and "the attempt logged apart" (7.2, step 4): it exercises the duplicate path itself, the outcome found before the version check, which is G4's "an ik-1 retry yields one revision and one audit event". That is why the record calls it "the stronger proof" and labels it simulated (7.2, 9, G6).

column1: Section 8 lists s0 and then s2, and appendix A gives the reason: act 1 changes nothing a take restores. Test that claim instead of taking it: list what act 1 leaves behind (7.1) and say why, under the reset's rules (6.7, 8), none of it matters to a take of act 2; then name a change to act 1 that would force an s1 into existence. Finally, argue why a fixture state is captured from a clean take's act end rather than written by hand as the next act's starting rows, and name the two checks that stop a state altered after its capture from being restored unnoticed.
column2: Act 1 leaves one session and one audit row and nothing else (7.1, act 1). The reset keeps every session and every audit row and deletes only rows committed after the state's point, so restoring s0 before act 2 removes nothing act 1 made, and act 2 starts from s0 too (8; 11.1, step 2). An s1 would be needed the moment act 1 committed a row a later act depends on, for example a space created on camera instead of by the provisioning script (6.7): a reset to s0 deletes every row past s0's point, so that row would be gone before act 2. A state captured from a clean take holds only rows the build's own code wrote, a revision 5 that admission accepted, a publication 1 the control plane wrote after Sarah's approval, under the build digest the state carries (8). Rows written by hand could hold something no mechanism produced, a publication with no approval behind it, and restoring them would put a state in front of the camera that no clean take reached. The reset itself is labeled, its audit event entering the rehearsal log as seeded state (9; appendix A's labeled step), but the act filmed after it is accepted as working, so it must start from rows a real take produced. The checks: the reset recomputes the state's digest, over manifest and build digest, against the pin file kept apart in the repository and refuses a mismatch with 412 (M3), and the recorder diffs each restored manifest, publication and approval digests included, against its capture (M4) (TH2, 8, 9).

column1: The canary suite must get a 404 for every replay, each paired with the owner's 200 for the same identifier in that take (R8, SR2). Say in one sentence which property the suite proves. TH4's preventative half already puts row-level security on every table: argue why the row still needs this detective half, naming one thing the suite can catch that row-level security cannot. Then describe two different broken setups, one in the build and one in the suite's own script, that a suite of bare 404s would pass and the paired suite would fail.
column2: It proves that nothing of Northstar's, data or metadata, reaches a session of another organization (G5, N7): it is TH4's detective half, M8, where SI1 is at stake, the platform's scope invariant that every read and write is scoped by the verified session's organization, never a request value (platform 10.2). Row-level security filters rows; it cannot see the rest of an answer. A handler that answers 403 where it should answer 404, or names the app in an error, tells the canary that Northstar's identifier exists without returning a single row, which is why R8 asks for denial "before data or metadata" and 5.1 for 404 rather than 403; and a policy missing from one table is a gap the preventative half cannot report about itself. The suite checks whole answers from outside, every take, so it sees both, which is why 10.4 gives every High row a preventative and a detective half. A broken build: a change that makes a route answer 404 to everyone, its owner included; the canary's 404 then proves only that the route is broken, and the owner's missing 200 fails the take. A broken script: replays built from the previous take's identifiers, which the reset deleted, so every replay is 404 because nothing exists; again no owner 200 in this take. In both a bare 404 cannot be told from a refusal, and the paired 200 is what proves the identifier was real and reachable by its owner at the time (R8, SR2, TH4; 11.1, steps 4 and 6).

column1: Rank three leaks from least to most damaging, and for each say what it yields and what bounds it: (a) a copy of the oauth_clients row taken from fAuth's database; (b) fAuth's platform key, leaked a week after provisioning; (c) the operator's machine, taken during act 5. Then explain why the platform key is the first of the operator's keys to be deleted.
column2: Least to most damaging: (b), (a), (c). (b) Nothing, if the rule was kept: the platform key creates tenants (appendix A, AS12) and "dies once the tenants exist" (10.6, M30), so a week after provisioning there is no key left to leak; it ranks first only because the rule held, and a key kept by mistake would be the power to create tenants at fAuth. (a) Next: the row holds no secret, only the client's registration and its one redirect URI (D9, 6.7). A code can be sent only to that URI, and redeeming one needs the code verifier the platform made for that one sign-in, which is never in the row (PKCE), so the copy signs nobody in; what remains is AR4, a wrong row added by hand, caught by the dry sign-in (M6). (c) Most: the machine holds every key still alive, the actors' sessions in their Chrome profiles, the raw export and the pin file at once (AS13, TH15), which is any principal in either organization and every operator power. It is bounded by M30 (fresh profiles destroyed after the last take, the raw file hashed, filtered and deleted in one step, full-disk encryption, the machine off the network except while a rehearsal runs), made visible afterwards by M31's anchored manifest, and the rest accepted (AR3). The platform key goes first because creating the tenants is the provisioning script's first fAuth step (6.7), so it is the first key whose job is over; the others still have work, the owner credential until its one run, fAuth's database credential until its one insert, the management keys until delivery (10.6). A key that will never be used again is only risk ("single use where possible", AR3).

column1: Diagram 03 runs Spend Review's command with no control plane, P3, on it, yet the workspace server checks every decision against the pinned publication's record schema, read from the publication row (F5). Argue why reading the row is as safe as asking P3, from who writes a publication and what it names (6.2). Then predict what migration step 4, one process to four services, would have to add if P2 asked P3 for that schema on every command instead, and which failure would then stop a decision that the design as written survives.
column2: Only role control writes a publication, inside the platform's SERIALIZABLE transaction, and a publication names one exact approved digest (6.2); a case stays pinned to its publication until an explicit adoption (R6). So the row cannot hold a schema P3 did not admit and publish, and it cannot change under a pinned case: asking P3 again would return the same answer, at the cost of a call, and the run path needs the database, not the control plane (7.2). If P2 asked P3 on every command, step 4 would turn that in-process call into a network hop on every decision, with its own request type and a principal carried across it, the things 11.1 says step 4 needs from D1, and the control plane's service would join the hard dependencies of every published app. Today the four roles share one process, so P3 cannot fail apart from P2; after step 4 it can, and a control-plane outage or deploy would then stop decision forms, where the design as written loses only what P3 itself does, admission and publication (6.2). That is what 7.2 means by "the control plane stays off the run path at migration (G7)" (7.2, 11.1).

column1: Rebuild the task's 8 GiB from its five parts, and the $85 Fargate line from the task's size and unit prices. Then rebuild the month of about $170 from its five lines and its $17 a rehearsal. Finally predict both numbers if the head asks for twenty rehearsals a month instead of ten, assuming the spike and margin stay at 40 generation attempts. Which line is the driver, and does it move?
column2: 1 GiB for the binary, 2 × 1 GiB for two DuckDB operations, the parser module's 2 GiB cap, the 2 GiB result cache and 1 GiB of headroom: 8 GiB. Fargate: 2 vCPU × 730 h × $0.04048 = $59.10, plus 8 GiB × 730 h × $0.004445 = $25.96, so $85.06. The month: $85 + $26 + $22 + $24 + $11 = $168, "about $170", and $16.80, about $17, a rehearsal at ten a month, $1.10 of it tokens. Tokens: 120 attempts are 2 attempts × 2 acts × 20 takes = 80, plus 40 for the spike and margin, at 8,000 tokens in and 3,000 out, $0.032 + $0.06 = $0.092 an attempt. At twenty rehearsals, 40 takes: 160 + 40 = 200 attempts, $18.40, so the month is about $175 and a rehearsal about $8.80. The driver is the Fargate line, and it does not move, because hosting runs whether or not anyone rehearses (11.2).

column1: Make the strongest case, in three sentences and with this record's own numbers, for recording on the founder's machine or a single virtual machine instead of the ECS task (D10's alternative): what it would save a month and a rehearsal, and what the scenes would lose by it. Then argue the other side from G7 and from what the founder's machine could never measure, and, before reading 13.2, predict the one measurement that should settle the host, and which result would move the demo off the task.
column2: For: on the founder's machine about $157 of the $168 month disappears, everything but the $11 of tokens, since a take's marginal cost is its tokens, "all the founder's machine (D10) costs" (11.2), so about $15.70 of each rehearsal's $16.80; a virtual machine needs no ECS account (12.2's table); one operator (A3) has one fewer system to provision and watch; and the restart the recording times is already a process restart under a supervisor (5.2), so the scenes lose nothing a task replacement would have shown. Against: the platform's own deployment is ECS on Fargate in one region, so a demo on the task is the platform's first deployment and its migration starts there, while a laptop or a virtual machine is a deployment to redo (G7). And the number the host question waits on, how long a full task replacement takes against N2's 30 s, can be measured only on the task: 5.2 leaves it unmeasured and times one apart, and the founder's machine "cannot time a task replacement" (12.2's table). So the deciding measurement is that one timed task replacement: if it meets N2's 30 s the task stays; if it misses, the host becomes one virtual machine, which is 13.2's current choice (5.2, 11.2, 12.2, 13.2).

column1: The second-app objection is answered by one fact: policy is per organization. Make the founder's best case for letting Maya publish Spend Review herself under owner publication, to save ten seconds; then show what that change would break elsewhere in the recording and what it would prove instead. Finally, if the provisioning script set owner publication by mistake, say what a check must compare the policy row against to catch it before the camera rolls, and why checking once, right after provisioning, would not be enough.
column2: For: Spend Review records internal decisions about synthetic expenses and pays nobody (7.2, step 6; 6.8's "no connector or external action"), so the founder can argue that a wrong decision costs little, that review adds only delay, and that ten seconds matter in a five-minute act. What it breaks: Security and Finance share Northstar's one policy row (6.2; 7.2, step 2), so owner publication for Spend Review is owner publication for the investigation app too; Maya's own publish in act 4 would succeed, and R4's refusal, the scene that proves independent review, would disappear (6.2's "act 4 loses its refusal"; RK4). What it would prove instead: that an administrator can set an owner-publication policy and the platform honours it, a claim about configurable policy rather than about a reviewer approving exactly what runs; and the partner would see an app nobody else approved, the very objection 13.3 answers. The check: the policy row against the provisioning script's manifest, the record of what the script meant to set, since the row alone cannot say it is wrong. Once is not enough, because the row can change after provisioning: the script is rerun when its output is wrong (11.4), and every reset restores rows from a captured state, so a wrong policy captured once comes back with each reset until the states are recaptured. That check is the pre-take assertion, reading each organization's one policy row against the manifest before every take (6.2; M10, as RK4 cites it), so a wrong kind stops the take before the camera rolls (R7, 13.3).
